title: I can code, but I can't draw. So I used AI to bring one of my old game ideas to life.
author: _Hauntlight_
selftext:
Hi everyone,

Like a lot of developers here, I have no problem writing code, etc., but I’m quite bad when it comes to UI/UX and asset creation.

Thanks to AI tools, I was able to bring one of my old ideas to life. I decided to use AI to handle the graphics, UI themes, and so on (even though it still required a huge amount of manual work that nobody ever talks about). It allowed me to deliver what I wanted in basically no time.

The game is a retro resource-management game where you play as a space station AI decision-support system during an alien contagion outbreak. You have 10 days to survive a quarantine while dealing with 150+ randomized events and working toward one of 15 unique endings.

With the help of AI, I also generated some fragments of the trailer below.

The game name is **Vesper-9: Containment Protocol** and is available to play in your browser (with a few bugs 😅) and on desktop.

Link to the free prototype:  
[https://hauntlight-real.itch.io/vesper-9-containment-protocol](https://hauntlight-real.itch.io/vesper-9-containment-protocol)

replies.author: _Hauntlight_
replies.body:
Hi!  
  
Basically, I used Gemini for image and video generation.

I generated the assets with the model and then edited them manually, mostly to remove things I didn’t ask for that the AI added on its own. I also described the UI I wanted, and it generated mockups of how it would look. I then used those images as a blueprint when building the actual interface. I built all of the interfaces usign gdscripts, so whenever I had any difficulties, I used Antigravity (Gemini 3.1 Pro) to help position and align elements correctly.

For the UI, my main challenge is translating what I have in mind into something practical. Having AI-generated blueprints makes that process much easier.

comments.author: Agreeable-Safety-360
comments.body: How'd you get such consistent art across your game?

replies.author: _Hauntlight_
replies.body:
I defined an art style metaprompt and used it at the end of each prompt.  It was similar to the following:

>2D digital art, sci-fi, dark atmosphere, flat UI perspective, pixel art and low-fi aesthetic, muted color palette with harsh neon accents, high contrast, minimalist.

I did everything in the same chat, but i do not know if it influenced the results.

comments.author: Independent9450
comments.body: There is something I am curious about the use of AI for game content generation. How do you guys usually handle copyright issues with AI generated graphics? I saw that OP uses nanobanana. I am asking since I am planing to start a new game and I am in the same position as OP.

replies.author: _Hauntlight_
replies.body:
This is one of the areas where the answer is "it depends". For Nano Banana there are really two separate questions:  
1. Are you allowed to use the generated images commercially? from a licensing perspective, using AI-generated images in a game is permitted, also commercially.

2. Do you actually own copyright in those images? This is complicated.

In the United States, the Copyright Office said that output created entirely by AI without sufficient (when is sufficient? Hard to tell!) human creative input are not eligible for copyright protection. If a human edits the output, the final work may be protected.

In Italy (and the EU), copyright law is based on the concept of "human authorship". There is currently no specific copyright category for fully AI-generated works. So I am not sure about whether a purely AI-generated image would receive copyright protection on its own. The legal trend in Europe is similar to the US: human creative coontribution decides.  
  
The biggest risk is that AI-generated content can still infringe someone else's copyright. If you generate something that is obviously derived from Mario, Pokémon, Disney characters, League of Legends artwork etc... and use it in your game the fact that an AI created it does not magically make it legal. You are still responsible for what you publish.  
  
My suggestion is to have human-created or heavily modified art for your game's core characters, logo etc... especially if you plan to sell it. What you could do (but it's not a guaranteed working technique is to basically ceate the asset, apply the needed changes and then try to usegoogle image to image search to understand if there is a really similar commercial asset that could represent a problem. It's not much but is the best you can do till we get a better law situation.
